transcript:
Meeting Header: 2026-07-28 15:00 UTC | Duration 42m | Attendees: Aisha Khan (Redwood AE), Diego Ramirez (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Venturis - Head of ML), Oliver Grant (Venturis - Platform), Priya Singh (Venturis - Security)

[00:00] Aisha Khan: Hi everyone, thanks for joining, um this is Aisha from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account. Diego from our infra/SE team is here as well.
[00:12] Maya Chen: Hey Aisha, hey Diego. Thanks, we've got Oliver and Priya on as well. We're excited to understand the model tradeoffs 
we've been evaluating a few open models and also looking at hosted vs dedicated.
[00:25] Diego Ramirez: Great, can you give a bit of context on your product and where LLMs fit in?
[00:30] Maya Chen: Sure. Venturis builds a multilingual insights platform for enterprise documents. We ingest docs in 8 languages, need semantic search, summarization and question answering. Latency targets are user-facing: under 500ms ideally for short queries, higher for long ops. We have an internal ranking pipeline that uses embeddings.
[00:48] Oliver Grant: We're also sensitive about cost 
we could start hosted but if cost per token is too high we might need dedicated reserved capacity.
[01:00] Aisha Khan: Totally makes sense. Quick qual 
approximate daily QPS and expected context lengths?
[01:06] Maya Chen: Right now prototype traffic is 50-100 QPS peak, mostly short prompts but we also do long-context summarization for docs up to ~50k tokens. For pilots we'd like to support 8k and 32k contexts, and evaluate feasibility for 128k later. Multilingual support is critical 
esspecially Chinese, Spanish, Portuguese and German.
[01:32] Diego Ramirez: OK so we should talk about model choices. Open models like Mistral and Mistral-Instruct variants, Mistral large 8x, or Llama-derivatives (open weights) vary in context length and tool-calling support. Also Redwood hosts curated open models and offers model variants optimized for latency/cost.
[01:55] Priya Singh: From security side we need SOC2, SSO (SAML), audit logs, KMS for key management and the ability to have private networking or VPC peering if we go private. How does Redwood handle data retention?
[02:12] Aisha Khan: Good question. For hosted we have configurable retention and data isolation controls; Dedicated gives reserved GPU pools with stronger isolation. Private deployments (VPC/on-prem) let you keep data entirely in your network. We also integrate with customer KMS for encryption at rest. We'll send the SOC2 pack after the call.
[02:33] Maya Chen: When you say 'tool-calling', do you mean function-calling like OpenAI's function call or more custom tool routing?
[02:40] Diego Ramirez: Both. Redwood supports function/tool calling and structured output. Some open models have varying support 
sometimes tool-calling requires a model that understands the function signature, so we recommend testing specific models.
[02:55] Maya Chen: And what about multilingual performance? Any benchmarks for Chinese and Spanish?
[03:02] Aisha Khan: We have per-model performance profiles; some open models are stronger on English, others are more balanced. We'll share our multilingual evals for similar customers but we'll also want a sample of your prompts to run targeted evals.
[03:18] Oliver Grant: Ok, can you talk about latency vs cost tradeoffs 
for our short queries under 500ms we're worried about serving costs at scale.
[03:27] Diego Ramirez: Sure. Short queries, small context: you can use smaller quantized model variants with low latency and lower cost. For long-context summarization we recommend models that support extended KV cache and optimized kernels 
those are higher cost per token but we can reduce billable tokens with prefix caching and chunking strategies. Also Dedicated reduces per-token cost if you commit capacity.
[03:50] Maya Chen: Are there recommended models for 32k contexts that also handle Chinese well?
[03:56] Diego Ramirez: There are a few candidates: some Llama derivatives with extended position embeddings, and new Mistral forks. The tradeoff is sometimes accuracy vs speed; we'll map candidates and run side-by-side evals on your prompt set.
[04:12] Priya Singh: For Private deployment, do you have an on-prem package? We have some regulatory customers who require air-gapped options.
[04:19] Aisha Khan: Yes, Redwood Private supports on-prem and VPC deployments. We can slot in the private control plane and ship an on-prem runtime; it includes audit logs and integrates with HSM/KMS. We'll share architecture docs.
[04:33] Maya Chen: Great. For the pilot, we'd like to test hosted first for speed of setup, and then dedicated if the economics make sense. Timeline wise, we'd like a pilot start in early September.
[04:44] Aisha Khan: Early September is reasonable; for that we should confirm success criteria 
accuracy thresholds, latency targets, cost per 1k tokens target, and languages.
[04:55] Maya Chen: Success criteria: 1) QA latency 90th pct under 750ms for short queries, 2) Summarization accuracy comparable to our current baseline (we'll provide evals), 3) Multi-lingual recall > 85% on our test set.
[05:10] Diego Ramirez: Noted. We'll need the sample prompt set and a few representative docs. That'll let us run model comparisons and cost estimates.
[05:18] Oliver Grant: About billing and quotas 
if we go hosted for the pilot and then switch to Dedicated, is there an easy migration path?
[05:25] Aisha Khan: Yes, same API and model pins. You can start hosted and then migrate to Dedicated with minimal code changes; we'll handle model rollouts and compatibility.
[05:34] Maya Chen: Any caveats about function/tool calling when moving from hosted to dedicated?
[05:40] Diego Ramirez: The runtime supports function-calling consistently; the main differences are performance tuning 
kernel selection and batching parameters can be tuned per deployment.
[05:49] Priya Singh: On compliance, do you log user prompts? We need redaction options and retention policies.
[05:56] Aisha Khan: We have configurable log retention and can opt out of full content logs; you can enable metadata-only logs or encrypted logs with customer KMS.
[06:06] Maya Chen: For model selection, could you run a quick set of recommendations now? We're leaning to an open model family that supports 32k and decent multilinguality.
[06:15] Diego Ramirez: Top-line: 1) If latency and cost are primary for short queries, evaluate quantized llama variants or smaller Mistral variants; 2) For 32k with strong multilinguality, evaluate Mistral-family extended weights or Alpine-like forks (we'll be specific in the follow-up); 3) For highest quality and tool-calling, some commercial models still win but you lose open-weight flexibility.
[06:45] Maya Chen: Any red flags re licensing? We prefer permissive licenses.
[06:50] Aisha Khan: We'll call out license types per model in the doc 
mit-like vs more restrictive.
[06:55] Oliver Grant: Can you provide an initial cost estimate for the pilot (50-100 QPS, mixed short and long)?
[07:02] Diego Ramirez: We'll run throughput/latency bench on a few target models against your QPS and context distribution; that'll give a ballpark. Dedicated monthly commit pricing will vary; we'll include example scenarios.
[07:16] Maya Chen: For multilingual support, will tokenization differ and impact cost? Chinese tokenization tends to be denser, right?
[07:23] Diego Ramirez: Yes tokenization and average tokens per doc vary by language and affect cost. We'll characterize per-language token counts in the benchmark.
[07:32] Priya Singh: Is there built-in RBAC and SSO? We need SAML and enforced role-based access.
[07:38] Aisha Khan: Yes, both for hosted and Dedicated/Private. In Private you can enforce your identity provider.
[07:44] Maya Chen: OK, question on tool-calling reliability 
sometimes models hallucinate function names or arguments. How do you mitigate?
[07:52] Diego Ramirez: We validate with structured output schemas, have robust post-parsing checks, and recommend model fine-tuning or few-shot templates for stability. Also Redwood's runtime can enforce function signatures to reduce hallucination.
[08:08] Aisha Khan: Quick pause 
are there other stakeholders we should include in the next meeting? Legal or procurement?
[08:14] Maya Chen: We'll loop in procurement for pricing and legal for license review; Priya will coordinate security docs.
[08:21] Priya Singh: Yup. Also need details on where logs live and exportability for audits.
[08:27] Aisha Khan: We'll include export formats and retention controls in the security pack.
[08:33] Diego Ramirez: For the technical deep dive, we propose a dedicated session covering: benchmarking results, deployment architecture for Dedicated/Private, and migration plan.
[08:42] Oliver Grant: Sounds good. Could you also include an example of prefix caching to reduce token costs?
[08:48] Diego Ramirez: Yes, we'll show caching strategies and how to configure automatic prefix/KV cache for common contexts. That can cut billable tokens significantly for repetitive queries.
[09:00] Maya Chen: One more 
for long-doc summarization with 50k tokens, what's the recommended approach? Chunk and summarize then synthesize?
[09:07] Diego Ramirez: Chunk-and-summarize is typical. We can also run retrieval-augmented generation with embeddings and iterative condensation. We'll test approaches on your sample docs.
[09:18] Aisha Khan: Closing loop 
next steps: we'll send the security pack and SOC2 artifacts, Diego will run initial latency/cost estimates and we'll set up a technical deep dive. Maya to send prompt set and sample docs.
[09:30] Maya Chen: Affirmative. I'll share prompts and a small doc set by Friday.
[09:36] Priya Singh: I'll review the SOC2 and share any additional compliance asks.
[09:40] Aisha Khan: Thanks all. Any final questions?
[09:44] Oliver Grant: None from me.
[09:46] Diego Ramirez: Quick note 
we'll aim to have the bench spreadsheet by next Tuesday.
[09:50] Aisha Khan: Perfect, I'll follow up with calendar invites for the deep dive and send the security pack.
[09:55] Maya Chen: Thanks Aisha, Diego. Bye.

End Transcript.
